title: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
summary: How FlashInfer unifies paged and radix KV caches as block-sparse matrices, composes shared-prefix attention with mergeable attention states, load-balances skewed batches with plan/run, and JIT-compiles variants.
outcomes: Build the kv_indptr, kv_indices and kv_last_page_len arrays for a paged batch and locate any token's page and slot
Explain why a page table is a block-sparse matrix and what gathering pages into shared memory costs
Merge partial attention states with the LSE operator and estimate cascade attention's memory savings
Compute FlashInfer's KV chunk size and work assignment for a skewed batch, and explain plan/run with CUDA graphs
Choose query tile sizes with GQA head fusion and explain how JIT-compiled variant functors fuse RoPE or soft-capping

lessons.title: Why LLM serving needs its own attention engine

blocks.md:
From the prerequisites you know two pieces. PagedAttention stores each request's KV cache in fixed-size pages listed in a block table, and FlashAttention computes exact attention tile by tile with online softmax so the score matrix never reaches HBM (the GPU's off-chip DRAM).

A serving engine needs both at once, and more. One batch can mix **prefill** (a whole prompt of query tokens), **decode** (one new query token per request) and **append** or chunked prefill (a few new tokens on top of an existing cache). Every request has a different KV length, and the lengths change every step.

Storage also varies. A vLLM-style page table groups tokens into pages (16 tokens in FlashInfer's cascade benchmarks), SGLang manages its radix-tree cache with pages of a single token, and requests that share a prompt could share its KV. On top of that come attention variants: grouped-query attention (GQA), sliding windows, logit soft-capping, custom masks, RoPE fused into the kernel.

The FlashInfer paper (Ye et al., MLSys 2025) observes that each serving system had built its own kernels for a subset of these cases. FlashInfer is one **attention engine** that serving frameworks such as SGLang, vLLM and MLC-Engine call into.

Why does decode behave so differently from prefill? The paper gives the operational intensity (FLOPs per byte moved) of FlashAttention in terms of the query length $l_{qo}$ and the KV length $l_{kv}$:

blocks.tex: I \;=\; O\!\left(\frac{1}{1/l_{qo} + 1/l_{kv}}\right) \;\approx\; O(l_{qo}) \quad (l_{qo} \le l_{kv}), \qquad I_{GQA} \approx O(g \cdot l_{qo}),\; g = H_{qo}/H_{kv}
blocks.caption: From Section 2.1 of the FlashInfer paper. With GQA, $g$ query heads share one KV head, so each loaded key and value is used $g$ times.

blocks.prompt: You batch 64 decode requests into one kernel launch. Does the operational intensity of the attention part go up compared with running them one at a time?
blocks.reveal: No. Each decode request has its own KV cache, so batching adds both work and bytes in the same proportion: intensity stays near $O(1)$ for $l_{qo} = 1$. The paper states this directly: batching does not alter the operational intensity. Batching helps the weight matmuls, not attention. What does raise it is reuse of the same KV by several queries: GQA (factor $g$), longer query chunks, or many requests reading one shared prefix. Lesson 3 exploits the last one.

blocks.title: FlashInfer: what is fixed at compile time vs known only at run time

scenes.caption: FlashInfer splits the problem in two. The variant, the KV layout and the task shape (head dims, page size, dtype) rarely change, so they are baked into a kernel at compile time.
Sequence lengths change every generation step. A lightweight CPU scheduler turns them into a work assignment for each thread block and stores it in a workspace buffer on the GPU.
The compiled kernel reads its work list from the workspace and the KV pages from the cache, and writes the output. The same kernel binary serves every step; only the plan data changes.

blocks.md:
The rest of the course follows the paper's three design ideas:

1. **One data structure**: every KV storage scheme is a block-sparse matrix (lesson 2), and shared prefixes use several such matrices composed together (lesson 3).
2. **One scheduler**: a load-balanced plan computed per step that still works with CUDA graphs (lesson 4).
3. **One template**: a customizable FlashAttention kernel specialized by JIT compilation (lesson 5).

Attention in serving is mostly about **memory traffic under irregular shapes**. FlashInfer's answer is to separate what is static (variant, layout, tile sizes: compile time) from what is dynamic (lengths, page lists: a cheap per-step plan).

blocks.question: A decode step for Llama-style GQA with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads. Ignoring other effects, how much does GQA raise attention's operational intensity over plain multi-head attention with the same query count?
options: About 4x, because each KV head serves $g = 4$ query heads
Not at all, decode is always $O(1)$
About 32x, one per query head
It depends only on the page size
blocks.explain: The group size is $g = H_{qo}/H_{kv} = 32/8 = 4$. Each key and value loaded from HBM is reused by 4 query heads, so intensity becomes $O(g \cdot l_{qo}) = O(4)$. Page size changes how KV is addressed, not how often each byte is reused.

blocks.question: Which of these does FlashInfer treat as run-time input to its scheduler rather than as a compile-time kernel parameter?
options: The head dimension
Whether logits are soft-capped
The KV length of each request in this step
The data type of the KV cache
blocks.explain: Head dimension, the variant (such as soft-capping) and dtypes are fixed when the kernel is JIT compiled. Per-request lengths change every step, so they go to the plan function, which produces a fresh work assignment without recompiling.

lessons.title: The page table is a block-sparse matrix

blocks.md:
Picture attention for a whole batch as one big matrix: rows are query tokens of all requests, columns are every KV slot in the GPU's cache pool. Request $i$'s queries may only attend to its own KV, so almost every entry is zero. The nonzeros come in rectangles: a group of query rows times one page of KV columns.

That is exactly a **Block Sparse Row (BSR)** matrix: a sparse matrix whose nonzeros are stored as dense $(B_r, B_c)$ blocks. In FlashInfer, $B_c$ is the page size chosen by the KV-cache manager and $B_r$ matches the kernel's query tile size. The paper's claim is that page tables, radix trees and token-level sparsity are all this one format with different block sizes.

BSR is indexed like CSR (compressed sparse row). FlashInfer's docs define three int32 arrays for a paged KV cache:

- `kv_indptr` (length batch + 1): request $i$ owns entries `kv_indptr[i]` to `kv_indptr[i+1]` of the next array.
- `kv_indices`: the physical page numbers, all requests concatenated.
- `kv_last_page_len` (length batch): how many slots of each request's last page are filled, between 1 and `page_size`.

Here is a toy batch with `page_size = 4` and KV lengths 10, 3 and 7. Every number below was computed with a script.

blocks.caption: The KV length formula from the FlashInfer KV-layout tutorial. Request 0: $4 \cdot (3-0-1) + 2 = 10$.

blocks.title: CSR page table for 3 requests, page_size 4

scenes.caption: Request 0 has 10 tokens, so it needs 3 pages (here physical pages 5, 1, 8, in any order the allocator chose). The last page holds $10 - 2 \cdot 4 = 2$ tokens.
Request 1 has 3 tokens: one page (page 3), partly full. Request 2 has 7 tokens: pages 0 and 6, last one holding 3. The indptr is a running sum of page counts: 0, 3, 4, 6.
Lookup: token 9 of request 0 is in entry $0 + \lfloor 9/4 \rfloor = 2$ of kv_indices, which is page 8, slot $9 \bmod 4 = 1$. Token 6 of request 2 is in entry $4 + 1 = 5$: page 6, slot 2.
Next decode step: every request appends one token. Each last page still has room, so only kv_last_page_len changes (to 3, 4, 4). The kernels see new lengths without any data movement.
One more step. Requests 1 and 2 had full last pages, so the engine allocates pages 2 and 4. Now indptr is 0, 3, 5, 8 and the last pages hold 4, 1, 1 tokens.

blocks.title: The same page table as a block-sparse matrix (tokens per page)

scenes.caption: Rows are requests (each row stands for that request's query tile), columns are the 9 physical pages. A nonzero block means the request reads that page; the value is how many of its 4 slots are valid.
kv_indices just lists the nonzero column blocks of each row, and kv_indptr says where each row's list starts. That is CSR over blocks, which is why FlashInfer calls the page table a BSR matrix.
Page size 1 (SGLang's token-level radix cache) is the same matrix with $B_c = 1$: one column per token. The FlashInfer 0.2 post calls this vector sparsity.

blocks.md:
How does a kernel run dense Tensor Core math on scattered pages? The paper's answer (Section 3.2.1): **gather into shared memory first**. Each thread block computes page addresses from `kv_indices`, copies those rows from global memory into a contiguous shared-memory tile, and from there the sparse and dense kernels are identical. The head dimension is contiguous in memory, so each row is fetched with wide, coalesced asynchronous copies (`LDGSTS`).

One Hopper feature does not fit: the TMA copy engine only handles fixed-stride (affine) addresses, so FlashInfer uses TMA for contiguous KV and falls back to Ampere-style async copies for paged KV.

blocks.code:
def kv_slot(r, t, kv_indptr, kv_indices, page_size):
    # where does token t of request r live in the paged cache?
    page = kv_indices[kv_indptr[r] + t // page_size]
    return page, t % page_size

kv_indptr  = [0, 3, 4, 6]
kv_indices = [5, 1, 8, 3, 0, 6]
print(kv_slot(0, 9, kv_indptr, kv_indices, 4))   # (8, 1)
print(kv_slot(2, 6, kv_indptr, kv_indices, 4))   # (6, 2)
# K for that token: k_cache[page, slot, kv_head, :]   (NHD layout)
blocks.caption: Reference version of the address computation each thread block does while gathering a K/V tile.

blocks.md:
What does the gather cost? The paper's Appendix B measured page-size-1 KV against contiguous KV on H100: within 1% for decode kernels and about 10% for prefill kernels, with the larger gap on the FA3 template, where dense loads can use TMA and sparse ones cannot. The FlashInfer 0.2 release post reports page-size-1 attention at about 90% of dense throughput.

Queries and outputs use the same idea without pages: a **ragged tensor** packs all requests' query tokens back to back with no padding, and `qo_indptr` marks where each request starts. In the docs' NHD layout, a single-tensor paged cache has shape `(max_num_pages, 2, page_size, num_kv_heads, head_dim)`, where 2 holds K and V.

Two classic bugs. First, `kv_last_page_len` is never 0: a request with exactly 8 tokens and page size 4 has 2 pages and last length 4. Second, FlashInfer does not allocate or free pages. Its FAQ says page-table management is the serving engine's job; FlashInfer only computes attention over whatever arrays you pass (int32, per the docs).

blocks.prompt: In the final scene above, request 1 grows from 5 to 6 tokens. Which of the three arrays change?
blocks.reveal: Only `kv_last_page_len`: request 1's last page (page 2) holds 1 token and has 3 free slots, so its entry goes from 1 to 2. `kv_indptr` and `kv_indices` change only when a request gains or loses a page.

blocks.question: A request has exactly 8 tokens in a cache with page_size 4. What are its page count and kv_last_page_len?
options: 3 pages, last_page_len 0
2 pages, last_page_len 0
2 pages, last_page_len 4
3 pages, last_page_len 4
blocks.explain: 8 tokens fill exactly 2 pages. The docs require $1 \le$ last_page_len $\le$ page_size, and the length formula gives $4 \cdot (2 - 1) + 4 = 8$. Writing 0 would describe a 4-token request; adding an empty third page wastes a whole page and breaks the formula.

blocks.question: Why can FlashInfer's FA3 (Hopper) kernel use TMA for contiguous KV but not for a page table with small pages?
options: TMA does not support FP16
TMA cannot write to shared memory
Paged KV is stored on the CPU
TMA only performs fixed-stride copies, while page gathers follow arbitrary indices
blocks.explain: The paper notes Hopper's TMA supports only affine, fixed-stride access patterns. A page table sends consecutive pages to arbitrary addresses, so the kernel computes each address from kv_indices and issues Ampere-style async copies, which costs registers and forces a smaller KV tile.

lessons.title: Attention states, cascade attention and composable formats

blocks.md: FlashAttention's online softmax already merges partial results block by block. FlashInfer makes that merge a first-class operation. For a query $q$ and a set $I$ of key positions, define the **attention state** as the pair $(O(I), \mathrm{LSE}(I))$: the attention output restricted to $I$, and the log-sum-exp of its scores.

blocks.tex: \mathrm{LSE}(I) = \log\sum_{i\in I} e^{q\cdot k_i}, \qquad O(I) = \sum_{i \in I} \frac{e^{q\cdot k_i}}{e^{\mathrm{LSE}(I)}}\, v_i
blocks.caption: Definitions from Section 2.2 of the paper (scores written without the $1/\sqrt{d}$ scale for brevity).
The merge operator $\oplus$ for disjoint $I$ and $J$. It is associative and commutative, so states can be merged in any order. Real kernels subtract the max before exponentiating for stability.

blocks.md: A tiny check, computed with a script: one query, 5 keys with scores 2.0, 1.0, 0.5, 3.0, 1.5 and scalar values 10, 20, 30, 40, 50. Split the keys into a prefix $I = \{0,1,2\}$ and a suffix $J = \{3,4\}$, compute each state separately, then merge.

blocks.title: Merging two partial attention states gives the exact answer

scenes.caption: Prefix only: $\mathrm{LSE}(I) = 2.4644$ and $O(I) = 15.117$. This is a correct attention output for a query that could only see keys 0 to 2.
Suffix only: $\mathrm{LSE}(J) = 3.2014$ and $O(J) = 41.824$. It was computed independently, possibly by a different kernel on different SMs.
Merge: the weights are $e^{2.4644}$ and $e^{3.2014}$ normalized, which is 0.3237 and 0.6763. So $O = 0.3237 \cdot 15.117 + 0.6763 \cdot 41.824 = 33.180$ and $\mathrm{LSE} = 3.5925$.
Ordinary softmax attention over all 5 keys gives 33.180 with LSE 3.5925, identical to the merge. No approximation was made.

blocks.md:
The paper adopts the attention state as the canonical output of every FlashInfer attention call, and $\oplus$ as the standard reduction, playing the role that summation plays in a matrix multiply. The library exposes it as `merge_state`, `merge_state_in_place` and `merge_states` in `flashinfer.cascade`.

This unlocks **cascade attention** (FlashInfer blog, February 2024). When many requests share a long prompt, run two kernels and merge:

1. A multi-query (prefill-style) kernel computes all requests' queries against the **shared prefix**. One thread block loads a prefix tile into shared memory once and every query in the block reuses it.
2. A batch decode kernel computes each query against its own **unique suffix**.
3. $\oplus$ combines the two states per query.

blocks.title: Cascade attention for a shared prefix

nodes.label:
Multi-query kernel
KV in shared memory

Batch decode kernel
KV via L2/HBM

scenes.caption: Without cascade, every request's decode thread block streams the whole prefix from HBM or L2 by itself. With B requests the prefix bytes are read about B times.
Cascade step 1: a prefill-style kernel puts many queries in one thread block, so each prefix tile is loaded into shared memory once and reused by all of them.
Step 2: the ordinary batch decode kernel handles each request's short unique suffix. Step 3: merging the two attention states gives exactly the full-attention output.

blocks.md: How much traffic does that save? A simplified model: count KV tokens read from HBM per decode step per layer, with $B$ requests, shared prefix length $P$ and suffix length $S$. Without cascade each request reads $P + S$ tokens. With cascade the prefix is read once (assuming all $B$ queries fit one query tile) plus $B$ suffixes.

blocks.caption: Example: $B = 32$, $P = 4096$, $S = 256$ gives $139264 / 12288 = 11.3$x fewer KV bytes. With 32 heads of dim 128 in FP16 that is 2176 MiB versus 192 MiB per layer per step.

blocks.title: Simplified HBM-read reduction from cascade attention

scenes.caption: P = 4096, S = 256: at B = 1 there is nothing to share (ratio 1). The ratio climbs with batch size toward $(P+S)/S = 17$. Simplified: ignores L2 hits, compute, and the cost of the merge.
P = 32768, S = 256: at B = 128 the model gives 64.5x. FlashInfer's blog measured up to 31x kernel speedup over vLLM PageAttention on H100 in this regime (B of 128 or more, suffix of 256 or less).
P = 1024, S = 512: long suffixes cap the benefit near 3x, matching the blog's finding that gains shrink as the unique suffix grows and the decode kernel dominates.

blocks.md: The paper generalizes this as **composable formats** (Section 3.1.2). Instead of one block-sparse matrix with one block size, store the KV sparsity pattern as a sum of several. Rows that share a prefix form a dense submatrix, so it goes into a format with a large $B_r$ (several queries per block, sharing shared memory); the rest uses $B_r = 1$. No KV data moves: only new `indptr` and `indices` arrays are computed over the same page pool.

blocks.title: Composable formats: 6 requests in 2 prefix groups

scenes.caption: Requests 0 to 2 share prefix pages s0, s1; requests 3 to 5 share s2, s3; each has one unique page u. In a single format with $B_r = 1$, each request's block loads its own 3 pages: 18 page loads (ignoring L2 hits).
Composable: the shared columns become blocks of size (3, 1), so one thread block loads each shared page once for 3 queries: 4 page loads instead of 12.
The unique pages stay in a $(1, 1)$ format: 6 more loads. Total 10 versus 18, and the two partial states per query are merged with $\oplus$.

blocks.code:
wrapper = flashinfer.MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper(2, workspace_buffer, "NHD")
qo_indptr_arr = [
    torch.tensor([0, batch_size], dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda:0"),  # level 0: shared prefix
    torch.arange(batch_size + 1, dtype=torch.int32, device="cuda:0"),   # level 1: unique suffixes
]
wrapper.plan(qo_indptr_arr,
             [shared_kv_page_indptr, unique_kv_page_indptr],
             [shared_kv_page_indices, unique_kv_page_indices],
             [shared_kv_last_page_len, unique_kv_last_page_len],
             num_qo_heads, num_kv_heads, head_dim, page_size)
o = wrapper.run(q, kv_cache)   # both levels read the same paged cache
blocks.caption: Abridged from the MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper example in the FlashInfer docs. Level 0 puts all queries in one row group over the prefix pages.

blocks.md: End to end, the paper tested composable formats in MLC-Engine for parallel generation (the OpenAI `n` parameter) on ShareGPT. Gains peaked at $n = 4$: inter-token latency fell 13.73% for Llama 3.1 8B and 17.42% for 70B. Very small $n$ did not benefit (blocks too small), and at large $n$ the gain plateaued because attention stopped dominating.

More levels are not free. The cascade API docs warn that adding levels is not always beneficial because of the overhead of merging attention results, and the paper notes real shared prefixes are often shorter than the long-prefix kernel benchmarks.

blocks.question: Partial states for one query: prefix $(O = 2.0, \mathrm{LSE} = 0)$ and suffix $(O = 6.0, \mathrm{LSE} = 0)$. What is the merged output?
options: 6.0, the larger LSE wins
It cannot be computed without the raw scores
blocks.explain: Equal LSEs mean both halves carry equal total softmax mass, so the weights are $e^0/(e^0+e^0) = 0.5$ each and $O = 0.5 \cdot 2 + 0.5 \cdot 6 = 4.0$. The merged LSE is $\log 2$. The states alone are enough; that is the whole point of the operator.

blocks.question: Which workload benefits LEAST from cascade attention?
options: 128 requests sharing a 32K-token document, 100-token answers so far
64 requests sharing a 4K system prompt with 256-token suffixes
4 requests sharing a 512-token prompt with 4K-token unique histories
256 parallel samples of one 8K prompt
blocks.explain: With $B = 4$, $P = 512$, $S = 4096$ the model gives $4 \cdot 4608 / (512 + 16384) = 1.09$x: the unique suffixes dominate the bytes and the merge adds overhead. The other three have long shared prefixes and large batches, the regime where the blog measured big speedups.

lessons.title: Load-balanced scheduling, plan and run, and CUDA graphs

blocks.md:
A decode batch rarely has equal lengths. If each request (or each query tile of a request) becomes one unit of work for one CTA (cooperative thread array, CUDA's thread block), the longest request decides when the kernel ends while most SMs sit idle. Flash-Decoding's fix is to split long KV sequences into chunks processed in parallel and merged afterwards; the merge is exactly the $\oplus$ from lesson 3.

FlashInfer's scheduler (Algorithm 1 in the paper, inspired by Stream-K) decides the chunk size and the assignment of chunks to CTAs from this step's lengths.

The algorithm, with query tile size $T_q$ and a fixed number of CTAs:

1. Give each work tile a cost $\alpha\, l_q + \beta\, l_{kv}$. In the shipping scheduler source the cost function is `2 * qo_len + kv_len`.
2. Compute a maximum KV chunk size $L_{kv}$ (below) and cut every query tile's KV into chunks of at most $L_{kv}$.
3. Sort chunks by length, longest first.
4. Repeatedly give the next chunk to the CTA with the least accumulated cost (a min-heap).

blocks.caption: Total KV work divided evenly over the CTAs. Toy decode batch: lengths 3000, 200, 400, 150, 1200, 250, so the sum is 5200; with 4 CTAs and $T_q = 1$, $L_{kv} = 1300$. This is Algorithm 1 as in the paper; the shipping persistent scheduler also rounds the limit up (to a multiple of 256).

scenes.caption: Naive: one work item per request, handed to whichever CTA frees up first. Request 0 (3000 tokens) keeps CTA 0 busy until 3002 while the others finish by 1354. Utilization is only 43%.

FlashInfer plan: request 0 is cut into chunks of 1300, 1300 and 400. Sorted longest first and given to the least-loaded CTA, everything finishes at 1354: 2.2x faster, 96% utilization (simplified cost model).

Request 0's three chunks produced three partial states (O, LSE) in the workspace. A contraction step merges them with $\oplus$; requests that were not split write straight to the output. The merge duration is not to scale.

blocks.md: Two details make this production-safe. First, **determinism**: Stream-K style kernels often combine partial results with atomic adds, whose order varies run to run. FlashInfer deliberately uses no atomics; the plan fixes which partials merge in which order, so identical lengths give identical outputs. Second, the **writethrough** optimization (Appendix D.2): only requests longer than total KV divided by #CTA get split, and the rest skip the workspace entirely.

blocks.prompt: Every request in the batch has the same KV length, and the batch has exactly as many requests as CTAs. What speedup does the balanced scheduler give over one-CTA-per-request?
blocks.reveal: Essentially none. $L_{kv}$ equals each request's length, nothing is split, and each CTA gets one equal item: the same schedule as the naive one. This matches the paper's kernel benchmarks, where FlashInfer's advantage over FlashAttention showed up mainly for **uniform and skewed** length distributions rather than constant ones.

blocks.md:
Now the API. Every attention wrapper splits its work into two calls, an **inspector-executor** pattern the paper borrows from irregular parallel computing:

- `plan(...)` runs on the CPU once per generation step. It takes the page-table arrays and head configuration, runs the scheduler, writes the plan into a pinned host buffer, and issues one `cudaMemcpyAsync` into the GPU workspace.
- `run(q, kv_cache)` launches the kernels. Because every layer of the model has the same lengths, one plan serves all layers.

blocks.title: One decode step with plan, run and a captured CUDA graph

scenes.caption: The engine updates its page table (new tokens, maybe new pages) and calls plan with kv_indptr, kv_indices and kv_last_page_len.
The work lists and the partial-to-final reduction map are copied asynchronously into fixed regions of the workspace. Their addresses never change between steps.
The engine replays a CUDA graph that contains run() for all layers. The graph was captured once; the kernels have a fixed grid and fixed pointers, and simply read the new plan from the workspace.
Next step: lengths change, so plan runs again on the CPU. Nothing is recaptured; plan itself is never inside the graph.

blocks.md: Why does this fit CUDA graphs, which freeze kernel arguments and grid sizes at capture? The paper's answer: both the attention and the contraction stage are **persistent kernels** whose grid size is fixed (by default a small multiple of the SM count), and each workspace section sits at a fixed offset sized for the worst case. Appendix D.3 bounds the partial-output section, since at most $2 \cdot \#\text{CTA}$ partial tiles need merging:

blocks.caption: $D+1$ holds the output vector plus its LSE. Example: 128 CTAs, $T_q = 16$, 32 heads, $D = 128$ gives $2 \cdot 128 \cdot 16 \cdot 32 \cdot 129 = 16{,}908{,}288$ values.

blocks.code:
workspace = torch.zeros(128 * 1024 * 1024, dtype=torch.uint8, device="cuda:0")
decode = flashinfer.BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper(workspace, "NHD")

# once per generation step (CPU side)
decode.plan(kv_page_indptr, kv_page_indices, kv_last_page_len,
            num_qo_heads, num_kv_heads, head_dim, page_size,
            pos_encoding_mode="NONE", data_type=torch.float16)

# once per layer, reusing the same plan
for i in range(num_layers):
    o = decode.run(q[i], kv_cache_at_layer[i])   # [batch, num_qo_heads, head_dim]
blocks.caption: Adapted from the BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper example in the FlashInfer docs (128 MB is the recommended workspace size). BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper adds qo_indptr and a causal flag.

blocks.md: The docs state that `plan()` cannot be used inside a CUDA graph or `torch.compile`. With `use_cuda_graph=True` the wrapper uses caller-provided index buffers and the batch size must stay fixed for its lifetime, so engines capture one graph per batch-size bucket. For bitwise batch-invariant decode output, the docs point to `fixed_split_size` or `disable_split_kv`.

blocks.question: An engine calls plan() before every layer's run() in a 32-layer model. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, plan must precede every run
plan() must be called only once at startup
run() will use the wrong KV pages
It repeats identical CPU scheduling 32 times per step, since all layers share the same lengths
blocks.explain: The plan depends only on the sequence lengths and page arrays, which are the same for every layer in a step. The docs and paper design plan for reuse across all layers; calling it per layer adds CPU overhead to every step. Calling it only at startup is also wrong, because lengths change every step.

blocks.question: Why does FlashInfer's split-KV reduction avoid atomic adds, unlike some Stream-K implementations?
options: Atomics are not available on Hopper
Atomic accumulation order varies between runs, so outputs would not be deterministic
Atomics would use too much workspace
LSE values cannot be added
blocks.explain: The paper says LLM serving requires deterministic outputs, so it dropped Stream-K's atomic aggregation. The plan fixes a reduction map, and the contraction kernel merges partial states in the same order every time the same lengths appear.

lessons.title: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants

blocks.md:
FlashInfer's kernels come from CUDA/CUTLASS templates: the FlashAttention-2 algorithm for GPUs up to Ada (sm89) and FlashAttention-3 on Hopper, per the paper. A classic FA2 kernel uses one tile shape such as $(128, 64)$ (query rows by KV columns), ideal for prefill but wasteful for decode, where a request has 1 query row.

So FlashInfer compiles FA2 kernels for query tiles $\{1, 16, 32, 64, 128\}$ times KV tiles $\{32, 64, 128\}$ and picks one per batch: the smallest query tile at least as large as the average (fused) query length, then the KV tile that maximizes SM occupancy under register and shared-memory limits. Query tile 1 uses CUDA cores because Tensor Core MMA needs at least 16 rows; FA3 tiles are multiples of 64 to fit Hopper's WGMMA.

What is a "fused" query length? Appendix A describes **head-group fusion** for GQA. Instead of one thread block per query head, FlashInfer maps one KV head to a thread block and stacks that group's query heads into the row dimension. A decode step with group size $g = 8$ therefore looks like a query of 8 rows against one KV stream: each KV tile is loaded into shared memory once and used by all 8 heads.

blocks.title: Head-group fusion: one KV head, its 4 query heads, 2 query tokens

scenes.caption: GQA with $g = 4$ query heads per KV head and 2 new query tokens (for example a speculative-decoding step). Simplified: the exact row order is an implementation detail.
Fused, this is one block of $2 \cdot 4 = 8$ query rows that all read the same KV head. The tile rule picks query tile 16, the smallest one of at least 8, which can run on Tensor Cores.
Without fusion each head would be a separate 2-row problem: query tile 16 would be 7/8 empty, and the KV head would be loaded 4 times.

blocks.question: A batch has average query length 3 per request and GQA group size 8. Which query tile size does FlashInfer's heuristic choose?
options: 32, the smallest tile of at least 3 x 8 = 24 rows
1, because it is mostly decode
16, the smallest Tensor Core tile
128, the prefill default
blocks.explain: With head-group fusion the effective query length is $3 \cdot 8 = 24$ rows. The rule takes the smallest tile meeting or exceeding it among 1, 16, 32, 64, 128, which is 32. Choosing 16 would need two tiles; 128 would waste most of the rows.

blocks.md:
The second customization axis is the attention **variant**. Inspired by FlexAttention, a FlashInfer variant is a small class of CUDA functors that the JIT compiler pastes into the kernel template:

- `QueryTransform`, `KeyTransform`, `ValueTransform`: applied to Q, K, V before attention (fuse RoPE, normalization or a projection).
- `LogitsTransform` and `LogitsMask`: modify or mask scores before softmax (soft-cap, ALiBi, sliding window, custom masks).
- `OutputTransform`: applied to the output.
- A `use_softmax` flag, so even non-softmax attention such as FlashSigmoid fits.

The paper summarizes the design space as $f_{epilogue}(\mathrm{scan}(f_{logits}(f_q(Q)\, f_k(K)))\, f_v(V))$.

blocks.title: A logits soft-cap variant inside the kernel (sketch)

scenes.caption: The variant is a C++ class given to the JIT compiler as a code string, in the style of the paper's Figure 5. Extra parameters such as cap become kernel arguments.
The constructor runs once per thread block and copies parameters into registers.
The generated kernel calls LogitsTransform on every score in its register tile. A score of 10 becomes $30\tanh(1/3) = 9.645$: small scores barely change.
A score of 50 becomes 27.933 and 100 becomes 29.924: large scores are squashed below 30, so one key cannot dominate. Then the usual online softmax runs.

blocks.caption: The soft-cap formula from the FlashInfer decode docs (used by Gemma-2 and Grok). Soft-capping is also built in as the logits_soft_cap argument of plan().

blocks.md:
Fusion is where variants pay off. The paper's StreamingLLM case study fused RoPE into attention with about 20 extra lines of query/key transform, cutting end-to-end inter-token latency by 28 to 30% and reaching 1.6 to 3.7x higher bandwidth utilization than separate RoPE plus attention kernels. On H100 it also reports higher TFLOPs/s than FlexAttention for causal, soft-cap and ALiBi variants, which it credits to warp specialization, TMA and register-level control that Triton did not fully expose.

JIT has a cost: kernels compile on first use and are cached. The 0.2 release reports all kernels for Llama models JIT-compile in about 15 seconds on server CPUs, and the README offers optional `flashinfer-cubin` and `flashinfer-jit-cache` packages with prebuilt kernels.

Where it stands and what it does not do:

- In SGLang on H100 the paper reports 29 to 69% lower inter-token latency than SGLang's Triton backend.
- In vLLM, FP8 KV cache gained about 13% ITL, but BF16 saw small regressions from host-side Python overhead in the integration (Appendix G.4).
- The paper's kernels are forward-only; training would need customizable backward templates.
- Wrappers take a `backend` argument; besides the FA2 and FA3 templates, the current docs list other implementations (for example cuDNN and TensorRT-LLM kernels) chosen automatically by GPU and workload.

FlashInfer = one block-sparse view of every KV layout, attention states merged with $\oplus$ so work can be split and composed freely, a per-step plan that balances skewed lengths while staying CUDA-graph friendly, and a JIT template so new variants get fused kernels instead of new libraries.

blocks.question: You want attention with RoPE applied inside the kernel (instead of a separate RoPE pass that writes rotated Q and K to HBM). Which variant hooks do you implement?
options: LogitsMask
OutputTransform
QueryTransform and KeyTransform
ValueTransform only
blocks.explain: RoPE rotates query and key vectors before their dot product, which is exactly what the query and key transform functors are for. The paper uses them for fused RoPE in StreamingLLM. A mask or output hook acts too late, and values are not rotated.

blocks.question: Why does FlashInfer pick a different query tile for decode than for long prefill instead of always using a large one?
options: Large tiles give wrong results for decode
A decode query has few rows, so a 128-row tile would be mostly padding and waste compute and shared memory
Small tiles have higher arithmetic intensity
Tile size must equal the page size
blocks.explain: Tile size affects efficiency, not correctness. With 1 to a few fused rows per request, a 128-row tile spends almost all of its work on empty rows. The paper notes the usual FA2 tile is good for prefill on A100 but inefficient for decode. Page size is independent of the query tile.
